posborne opened PR #15101 from posborne:resource-table-host-heap-limiter to bytecodealliance:main:

Motivation

Embedders currently lack an aggregate host-side memory boundary for component model resources in ResourceTable. While #12652 added mitigations around handle counts and hostcall fuel, cumulative host heap allocations owned by resources in ResourceTable were previously untracked by any umbrella mechanism.

Over the past several releases, Wasmtime has had to address a recurring class of guest-driven host memory exhaustion advisories with mitigations including [GHSA-852m-cvvp-9p4w] and [GHSA-243v-98vx-264h] (#12652), [GHSA-c9gc-w9vx-w86p], [GHSA-gqmc-89g8-p25r], and [GHSA-6fr9-xmw9-5352]. While per-resource and per-call limits help, they do not bound the aggregate host heap memory accumulated across entries in a ResourceTable.

Solution

This PR adds host heap usage accounting and optional per-table byte limits to wasmtime::component::ResourceTable. This provides a level of umbrella coverage to protect against host paths that may not have protections currently and to provide a higher level limit that is easier to reason about for embedders.

The way that this is achieved involves the introduction of a HostHeapUsage trait which is required for all resources. This is accompanied by a FixedHostHeapUsage trait as a marker for types which do not contain children with heap storage not accounted for in their own size directly. Methods on the table that push, delete or mutate (update) resources use the traits to account for the heap usage changes associated with the operation. If a limit is set and an operation causes the heap usage to grow beyond the set limit, the operations return an error which will typically result in a guest-side trap.

These new requirements necessitate updates across the wasmtime tree and will be a breaking change for embedders that are pushing their own resources into ResourceTables.

Design Decisions

The code here has gone through a few iterations and updates based on discussion in #12984. What is present here tries to incorporate that feedback and is closer to some of the implementation from servo/firefox/stylo MallocSizeOf trait.

In instrumenting the code to implement the traits, I decided that to ease the burden on embedders and to provide some additional static guarantees, it would be beneficial to introduce proc-macros in order to aid in deriving the traits on compatible structs and enums.

For mutation I went with a closure-based update rather than a guard, because the limit check has to be fallible and a guard could only account in Drop. This makes former get_mut call sites a bit noisier. Since update can only measure after the mutation runs, growth past the limit is reported rather than prevented, and the mutation isn't rolled back because the error is expected to trap. The overshoot is roughly limited to what a single host call can allocate.

Across the code in tree (mostly wasi p2/p3), I tried to provide pragmatic implementations of the trait where reasonable and erred on the side of overcounting bytes in most cases. There are some reference counted cases which are not tracked with complete accuracy but, even in those cases, abuse should be challenging as the fixed size of the resource will be counted even if the amortized cost of the shared data is left unaccounted.

Future Work

The changes here are sprawling, so I wanted to avoid increasing the scope beyond what was required for purpose and reasonable ergonomics (adding derive). Potential future work that I opted to not try to incorporate here include:

  • Allow for the limit to be set at a higher level outside of individual tables, probably on the ResourceLimiter.
  • Hooks to intervene when limits are exceeded or at watermarks prior to the limit.
  • Fast path or conditional compilation to opt out of tracking; even if no limit is set the accounting is done and count is available.

Closes #12984

Thanks for this! I personally think this is a pretty reasonable change to make and it's only going to be even more accurate than things are today if embedders conservatively always use FixedHostHeapUsage. By providing the knobs though I think this is going to be quite useful.

That'd help with rightward drift and it would have the same rough semantics for the borrows. I think it would require a small bit of unsafe code and/or a raw pointer to simultaneously hold the table and the entry pointer, but that seems like it's likely going to be worthwhile given the ergonomic wins.

I can add a comment; the reasoning is basically that, it isn't possibly to guarantee that in all cases the tracking could never get off in some way with out of band mutations. Saturating rather than underflow seemed like the more pragmatic and safe option here; bubbling up an error that will guest-trap could be another option but that feels heavy-handed.

:speech_balloon: posborne created PR review comment:

This is the approach I originally wanted to go; the problem with that is that when limits are exceeded the behavior we want is to raise an error that will result in a guest trap rather than a host trap. So Drop isn't a great option there unless there's a trick I haven't thought through.

Having a finish() consuming self explicitly can make that explicit but doesn't statically avoid the Drop and when I had used it in a few places, it generally didn't make things easier to write, so I ended up consolidating on the closure-based approach instead for this case.
:memo: posborne submitted PR review.

:speech_balloon: posborne created PR review comment:

I agree; I wasn't too happy to leave these and should have had a comment as to why they were omitted. The reason isn't the best, but it's basically that I had trouble thinking through exactly how we'd track these in all cases. There are some other specific protections here, but having it not included in the umbrella isn't ideal.

There is tracking taking place, even for FixedHostHeapUsage, but it is just the size of the struct itself without following the boxed types, so it is better than nothing and would catch the most naive runaway usage attempts.

The other bad thing here is that since this table is internal, I don't think embedders will often be aware that this extra table even exists and is performing host allocations. It might not even be possible to get a reference to the table to set a limit on it as an embedder (though I would need to double check that). That's probably best solved by wiring up the limits to coalesce at a higher level.
:memo: posborne submitted PR review.

:speech_balloon: posborne created PR review comment:

I would have liked to have an impl for Box<T> and attempted it. A Box<T> where T: HostHeapUsage + ?Sized impl conflicts with

impl<T: FixedHostHeapUsage> HostHeapUsage for T { ... }

because Box is #[fundamental], so a downstream crate could implement FixedHostHeapUsage for Box<MyType> and overlap with it (E0119).

The way to get a generic Box<T> is to drop that blanket impl, so fixed types would need an explicit HostHeapUsage impl alongside FixedHostHeapUsage. #[derive(FixedHostHeapUsage)] can emit both, so derived types are unaffected. The hand-written impl FixedHostHeapUsage for X {} sites would need a second impl, which a small helper macro could cover (e.g. impl_fixed_host_heap_usage!(MyType)).

Honestly, I wasn't quite sure which direction to go with this one, so happy to hear any suggestion you might have.

:speech_balloon: posborne created PR review comment:

Yeah, we can make it work by giving it the extra attribute required for bits that are within the wasmtime crate itself.

#[derive(FixedHostHeapUsage)]
#[component(wasmtime_crate = crate)]
struct TaskGroup {
    ref_count: usize,
}

Some of these sites were ones that I had written prior to adding the proc-macro; I can probably just do a conversion of to use the proc-macro for all sites where it can be applied. That gives us a bit more confidence that those impls are safe which makes auditing easier.

:speech_balloon: alexcrichton created PR review comment:

Oh right sorry yes I remember now that was in the OP and forgot about that when re-reading this. That's a good point too!

Subjectively I place a high value on preventing rightward-drift and using RAII wherever possible, so I'm tempted nevertheless to push on this. What would you think about something like:

  • An explicit finish which returns Result
  • Changing Drop to flag a table as "over capacity" to yield an error on next-access

That way embedders can get eager traps if they want, but otherwise natural access of the table would still handle this error case at least eventually. My thinking is that update is already sort of catching a sin that's already been committed as opposed to preventing it from happening in the first place, so delaying that error a bit longer probably isn't the worst in the world.

xia-chao commented on PR #15101:

While investigating wasi-http fields memory I found that with current defaults, 25k fields × 120 KiB in a 3 GiB cgroup gets OOM-killed (rc=137). This PR adds the API; do you plan a CLI default too?
:memo: posborne submitted PR review.

:speech_balloon: posborne created PR review comment:

I'm trialing a version of the change that goes this direction (single trait and RAII access patterns). I _think_ it will work and we can trap at the right places, though I need to play with a few options there: at the head of future subsequent mutating access blocks is the obvious instrumentation point (which we already have in some places), but I think there may also be a way to do the check at the point we're about to re-enter guests; that would mean that we trap without having to make another subsequent hostcall, which seems like what you would want. We'll lose a little visibility into which table change pushed things over the limit, but I generally expect that this will either be unimportant or obvious from context (and solvable if we decide it matters).

This should allow for most of the table accesses to go back to the upstream form which should make review a bit easier.

:speech_balloon: posborne created PR review comment:

I'll go through and resolve comments once I have changed vetted and on the branch, but I am moving toward making it so that we can apply the proc-macro (over the single HostHeapUsage trait) in almost all cases.

The macro will have attributes for the common cases we seem to encounter, currently thinking something like these:

fn dynamic_size(field: &MyType) -> usize {
    // ...
    42
}

struct MyStruct {
    #[heap_usage(shared)]
    shared: Arc<SomeType>, // where SomeType: HostHeapUsage.  Will include the size of SomeType for this field.

    #[heap_usage(constant = 42)]
    fixed_opaque: OpaqueFixed, // some type that we can account for with a fixed value (expr)

    #[heap_usage(skip = "reason skipping is reasonable")]
    zero_size: Opaque,

    #[heap_usage(with = dynamic_size)]
    dynamic: MyType, // MyType doesn't/can't impl HostHeapUsage
}
